canonical_statement: The review summarizes mechanisms of ESR1 mutation-mediated endocrine resistance and analyzes how ESR1 mutations affect outcomes with ER-targeted agents and combination therapies in metastatic hormone receptor-positive breast cancer.

The review reports that ESR1 mutations occur in approximately 20–40% of patients after aromatase inhibition for metastatic breast cancer, compared with 4–5% after adjuvant aromatase inhibition, 1.5–7% after neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition, and less than 1% in endocrine-therapy-naive metastatic disease.

The review reports that about 50% of endocrine-resistance cases are associated with an ESR1 mutation, while other resistance mechanisms include PI3K-AKT-mTORC1, RAS-MAPK, and CDK4/6-RB-E2F pathway alterations and ESR1 loss, amplification, or translocation.

The review describes tissue biopsy, circulating tumor cells, and cell-free DNA as sample sources for ESR1 testing, with next-generation sequencing and droplet digital PCR as detection methods and droplet digital PCR described as the most sensitive.
The review identifies D538G and Y537S as the most common ESR1 ligand-binding-domain resistance mutations and reports polyclonality in approximately 20–70% of patients in cell-free-DNA studies.

The review characterizes three findings as well established: ESR1 mutations are acquired during aromatase-inhibitor treatment in the metastatic setting, predict resistance to aromatase-inhibitor monotherapy, and lack prospective evidence establishing how mutation status should be incorporated into clinical decisions.
Ligand-binding-domain-mutated ESR1 is constitutively active and therefore is not suppressed by aromatase-inhibitor depletion of estrogen.

Although ESR1 mutations show relative tamoxifen resistance in preclinical models, the review notes that ESR1 mutations are not enriched after tamoxifen monotherapy or in tamoxifen-resistant metastatic breast cancer and therefore were not established as a major clinical mechanism of tamoxifen resistance.

canonical_statement: The review concludes that ESR1-MUT can blunt the efficacy of PI3K or mTORC1 inhibitor combinations when the endocrine backbone is an aromatase inhibitor because the mutation nullifies that aromatase-inhibitor component.

The review identifies mutation-specific effects, cfDNA-guided treatment switching, superiority of novel ER-targeted agents, ESR1 interactions with PI3K-AKT-mTORC1 signaling, ESR1 fusion treatment, and experimental modeling of combinatorial resistance as major open questions.
